utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in the courtroom, to those who are listening and watching the procedure. The witness should be brought in, please. Just for the record, the Chamber is sitting with two Judges pursuant to Rule 15 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Welcome back to the courtroom. I have to remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth you made at the beginning of your testimony yesterday still applies. Mr. Vanderpuye has more questions for you. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning to you, Your Honours; good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And good morning to you, Colonel. I wanted to clarify something before we move on in the record. Yesterday, I have it at page 67 in the transcript, you were commenting on how long a period had elapsed between the time you received this direction to prepare the Batkovic prison and the time it was that you called General Tolimir because the prisoners hadn't arrived, and in lines 18 through 20 of the transcript, your recorded as having said in regards to our discussion about this: "That is why I conclude that it was more than 24 hours. I'm not saying this because I'm certain it was 30 hours." And then it says "though," t-h-o-u-g-h, "or five days." I just want to clarify with you. Did you actually ever say "five days" in that context?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have perfect memory, but when I was explaining it, I was trying to make a point that it could not have been less than 24 hours. I explained that some work had already been done in terms of emptying the building and all the wheat taken out. It could not have been done in less than 24 hours. It took some time for the task to be conveyed and those responsible at the farm to organise themselves. It all needed at least 24 hours or more, so I made a reference to a few days. In our language, it could mean two, three, or up to five days. I don't know if I said five days exactly, but in any case, several days and more than 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm glad I asked you that, and the reason is because in your interview you haven't mentioned anything more than 48 hours. Would you agree that that's the case?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat, I don't have a perfect memory of what I said. I didn't come with any answers prepared beforehand. I provide honest answers, and I'm trying as best as I can to recall as many details as possible. It was more than 24 hours. Whether it was two, three days, or even five days, that is something I can't tell you from this position.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I appreciate that, but my question is whether during the course of your interview on the 2nd of February, 2010, or the 3rd of February, 2010, you ever mentioned that the period of time between when you received this task and when you called General Tolimir with respect to it, that you never mentioned that it was anything more than 48 hours. Would you agree that that's the case? I'm not asking you about your present recollection of the events. I'm asking about what's in your statement that you acknowledged and stood by yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read the transcript that was given to me of my interview of the 2nd of February, 2010, although not in detail. I didn't study it in detail intentionally so as not to provide identical answers, so as to appear that I have prepared myself or that I was prepared by someone else as to what I would say or change. That is why I'm trying to speak spontaneously and responsibly, because I'm trying to recall as many details as possible in answers to your questions. I accept that in the interview I may have mentioned the figures of 24 or 48 hours. Much as I'm saying now, it was more than one day and up to a few days. Forty-eight hours is two days. In our language it can frequently be within a given span that need not translate accurately into different languages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, I think you receive the answer I think now two or three times. There is no need for repetition, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I do want to advise the Court that in light of the witness's answers I will be tendering that transcript because I think it is important for the Court to see what it is the witness has testified to -- or, rather, has stated previously in contrast to what the witness is testifying to before the Trial Chamber, particularly since the witness now claims that he doesn't have a present recollection of the statement itself as opposed to the events. That's the reason why I've put the questions to him, and I think the record is clear on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yesterday we left off and I was asking you about the Vanikov Mlin prison. Do you remember that, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in particular, I asked you whether it was the case, or not, if members of the Main Staff security administration brought prisoners to that facility. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember -- well, I can't be specific. I think I said yesterday that it could have been on the 12th or the 13th. In any case, a few days following the fall of Srebrenica. A certain number of Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina members, probably from the Srebrenica area, were brought in by the intelligence organs of the security administration of the Main Staff. They brought them in, and they conducted interviews with them in Bijeljina in Vanikov Mlin.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: How many people do you recall were brought to that facility by the Main Staff security administration to be interviewed or questioned?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not a matter of my recollection. I didn't know then, and I don't know now, since the superior command was not under an obligation to inform me of either the numbers of those people or the contents of their interviews. I simply say that a number of them was brought in, but I don't know anything more specific than that. I remember a single name of a person from that group for other reasons, but you have to put me a question if you need to know why and who that person was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'll put that question to you in a moment, but how many people do you recall roughly? Was it a large number of people? Forty, 50 people? Ten or 12 people? Can you give us an approximation to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the number was not great. I don't know what to say exactly. Ten, 12, 13. These were human beings, not objects. Therefore, I don't want to speculate with numbers. There weren't that many. Perhaps around ten, conditionally speaking. I don't know exactly. Since -- since we're discussing this topic, I suppose they were, in a way, in agreement with being interviewed. You know what the situation must have been like. If you are in dire straits, you may well consent to giving an interview just to get out of trouble. I don't know what was going on exactly. I suppose -- or, rather, I'm relatively certain that in the log-book of the detention unit at Vanikov Mlin, there must be the names of those held there, and if needed, it could be checked with the prison warden who is still alive, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Who from the Main Staff brought these prisoners to that facility to be interviewed? Who from the security administration of the Main Staff escorted these prisoners or interviewed them?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a difficult question. That is difficult to answer. Who brought them in? I don't know, not for sure, given that some members of the intelligence organ were also in Bijeljina in their intelligence sub-centre. They acted as hosts, so to speak for -- for those interviews. It was announced to them, and they were included in the whole thing. I don't know who in the chain was responsible for bringing those people in and who organised the interviews. At that time, as well as at other times, I had a number of my own tasks to tackle, so I didn't get involved if it wasn't necessary. The Drina Corps command had two forward points in Brcko and Majevica. I had to go there daily, collect information, issue instructions. I had to be present there physically, and I was under an obligation to perform all those tasks, although I had a very small number of staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter -- or, rather, P2176 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document in Serbian is quite illegible.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I have a hard copy of it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The registrar just printed out a hard copy. It may be given to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Are you able to read the document now, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, are you able to read the document now? I'm asking you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm trying to make out the sense of the first two rows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That was not the question. If you are able to read it. Is it legible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hardly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to everyone. Mr. President, I think on the Prosecution list there is a 65 ter document number 7321. I believe that version of this same document is quite legible. Perhaps we could try placing that one on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It seems to be a bit better. And perhaps the registrar could print it and give a hard copy to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can read from the monitor too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, thank you for your assistance. Mr. Vanderpuye, carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If the witness can't read it, I have, I think, a legible copy in B/C/S in my hand, so if that becomes a problem we should be able to go forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In any event, Witness, you can see that this document is from the Main Staff, from the sector for security and intelligence affairs, the security administration, and is directed to the security department of the Eastern Bosnia Corps. That would be your department. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The copy I have now is legible, and if I may, I'd like to go through it to jog my memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please answer first the question that Mr. Vanderpuye put to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apologies. I wasn't paying attention enough. I was looking at the page, and I overheard the question. Could you repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It is directed to the security department, East Bosnia Corps. That would be your department. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In the body of this document -- well, first we should go -- you can see on your page, if we go to the -- all right. It's on the first page in any event. We can see this is signed by Naval Captain Ljubisa Beara. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Are you familiar with Naval Captain Ljubisa Beara?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am, but I see something that is illogical on this document. In the heading it says the --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... We can just go with the questions first, and we'll get to your issues, okay? If that's all right.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What was his position in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the chief of the security administration as part of the intelligence and security sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in this document we see a very specific reference to an individual code-named Atlantida. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In this document, it reads that: "Since the current accommodation of Atlantida is not appropriate and has raised public attention and in view of the fact that we need Atlantida to point out possible directions and sources for further collection of documents and in order to file criminal charges against criminals, it is necessary to secretly transfer Atlantida in the night of 10 to 11 June," as it's recorded here, "1995 or some other suitable time to the Mlin Military Prison in Bijeljina." That would be the facility that we've been just talking about. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's the facility that's secured by members of the military police battalion of the East Bosnia Corps over whom you had specialist control; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, along professional lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Specialist or professional control are different terms, and I'd kindly like to ask the Prosecutor to bear that in mind when putting questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please carry on, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You can see further in this -- in the second paragraph of this document that it says: "Captain Carkic will make arrangements for this with the brigade commander, Major Rajko Kusic, and personally carry out the task by notifying OB security organ of the East Bosnia Corps Chief Colonel Todorovic about his arrival and will be -- and will in personal contact explain our requests." Do you see that? Do you see that, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that. I am comparing the legible with the illegible version.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Are you the Colonel --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Are you the Colonel Todorovic that's referred to in this document?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you know who this Captain Carkic is who's referred to in this document?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose it was someone from up there. I can't remember his face or name, but if he introduced himself to me at that time as Captain Carkic, then I accepted him as such, especially because prior to his arrival I had received a telegram notifying me of that. But either before that or after that, that name and rank didn't mean much to me because he wasn't from my unit. My task based on this was something I probably did through the garrison commander, and that was to provide accommodation for him and security. That's the scope of my activities concerning this issue and the code-name Atlantis. It probably referred to someone who was not from my unit. Otherwise, I could probably recall a name or a person. In any case, I don't know what Atlantida stands for, who the person in question is. It was my task to provide accommodation and to provide conditions for the official work that had to be done, which is something I probably did through the garrison commander. I probably called him and told him to provide an off -- an office, a space where someone would come in and work once they arrived from the Main Staff. There is an illogical matter, though, which might be a typographical error. It seems it was drafted on the 10th of August, but it says that during the night between the 10th and the 11th of July -- or June it was supposed to take place. This doesn't make sense. So it was probably between the 10th and the 11th of August. And there seems to be something wrong with the signature. It says "Sector for security and intelligence." The chief of that sector was General Tolimir and not Naval Captain Ljubisa Beara. He was only chief of the security administration that was part of the sector. It may be a formality, but I don't know how important it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I appreciate that information, and in fact, the Trial Chamber has received information -- or evidence, I should say, concerning the date upon which Atlantida was transferred to the Mlin Military Prison that we've spoken about. Now, do you have information that the Atlantida that's referred to in this document was Colonel Avdo Palic, commander of the Zepa Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, the subsequent sequence of events pointed toward that logical conclusion that the person in question may have been Colonel Avdo Palic. I can explain if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Explain how it is that you know that Atlantida is Colonel Palic.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know, nor have I said that I know now, but that's a logical inference I make, because after this date -- I don't remember exactly which date it was. You showed me a document in which that date is mentioned. During the night, that's when I learned his name, Major Pecanac, Dragomir Pecanac or Dragoljub Pecanac, came to fetch Colonel Palic. He came from the security administration of the Main Staff. He arrived to take away Avdo Palic from the military detention centre to Vanikov Mlin, to the Main Staff. Since the warden of the military detention centre didn't know Pecanac personally, Major Pecanac, it seems suspicious to him that somebody should arrive in the middle of the night and take away a prisoner, so that the prison warden, Milan Savic, was -- was in a -- in an uncomfortable situation. During that period, round about midnight or shortly after midnight - certainly it was very late and I was asleep in bed - he called me up and asked me, "Buddy," he didn't even address me as Colonel, he said, "Buddy, I've got a problem." And I asked him, "What kind of problem. I'm sure it's a problem given the fact you're calling me at this hour." And he said, "You know, the one who is in detention here, the VIP," he wouldn't say his name. Although at the time as far as I remember, I didn't really know the name nor was I especially interested. He said, "Some major arrived. He says his name is Pecanac and that he's from the security and intelligence administration of the Main Staff, and he wants to take him there, to the Main Staff." And I asked him, "So what's the problem? Is it -- is the person there, prisoner?" And he answered, "Yes, it's their prison." And I said, "So, what's the problem?" And he answered, "The problem is that he doesn't want to sign" that he took over the detained person, Avdo Palic, at such and such an hour. And I said, "Of course you must do it, because it's not a glass of water that you can just give anybody without registering it." And he says, "Yes. That's what I told him, but he won't do it. He's standing right next to me. Maybe you want to talk to him." And he gave me Major Pecanac on the phone. I asked him, "Well, Pecko," I called him that because we knew each other personally. "What's the problem, Pecko?" And then he started beating about the bush. I said, "There's nothing to discuss. Sign in the log-book if you want to take the person with you and if you've come in an official capacity. If not, come again tomorrow during office hours and now go back where you came from. All right?" And after 10 or 15 minutes he either called me up again or possibly Savic told me right away that he had signed and taken Avdo Palic with him. So that I suppose -- or, rather, it's a logical inference I make that the person whose code-name was Atlantida was, in fact, Avdo Palic. If he was taken away after the 10th of August, and it probably is, because we saw the dates in that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I want to show you a document. It's 65 ter 7330.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is one of these documents that didn't have a 65 ter number. It bears directly on the witness's current testimony as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I raise the matter that we have two different versions of the same document just in front of us. That was P1267 and 65 ter 7231. The second one was better legible. Perhaps you may replace the illegible by the better one, the 65 ter document, and then it will be in evidence with a P number.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. That's a good idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The document that I want to show this witness now, Mr. President, is directly related to his testimony concerning the pick-up, as it were, of Colonel Palic by Captain Pecanac. I think it's important for the Trial Chamber to receive it. I don't know whether or not General Tolimir has an objection to it. I've alerted them, obviously, to the potential use of this document, and so far I've heard no objection with respect to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you see the document in front of you, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it. Need I say anything about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Not just yet, but it is entitled "Bijeljina garrison command, garrison prison"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If you hadn't said so yourself, I would have pointed that out, because in my evidence yesterday, I said that the garrison command also had a garrison detention centre which is in an organisation unit of the corps command, and it doesn't have much to do with my professional line of business.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The document itself appears to be a receipt. It says "Receipt" on it, and it says: "On the exclusion of the detainees on the 5th of September 1995 at 0100 hours for the needs of the," as it's translated, "organisation intelligence sector of the VRS Main Staff for the investigation." And then it says: "Palic Avdo, prisoner of war. "Transferred following the order of Tomic Draga, officer on duty of the Eastern Bosnia Corps intelligence organ." Now, Tomic Draga would be one of your assistants, wouldn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but let me tell you, this is no exclusion of any kind. This form was printed by the people at the time, and they weren't very versed in linguistical things. Actually, it's a receipt for prisoners handed over from the prison. So it's a receipt that some person is no longer in prison but has been taken away somewhere else. So the word "exclusion" is not the best here. And as I said, this was made for the needs of the sector of the security and intelligence of the Main Staff of the VRS. This prison warden, Milan Savic, first talked to my duty officer, because in my department there were duty shifts round the clock. So he talked to the duty officer, and the duty officer checked whether Pecanac had really come to fetch him. He called up the duty officer at the Main Staff and told Savic, "Hand him over to Pecanac," or, "Let Pecanac take him over and take him away, because he really is a man from the Main Staff." But Milan Savic is elderly man, and that is why he was in that position. I explained to you how we selected the police officers both for Batkovic and for the military detention centre. He was very responsible, and he knew me personally. So he wanted to make sure, and therefore he asked me, he double-checked with me whether Pecanac was really an authorised person so as to avoid making a mistake - Savic, I mean - for which he could be held accountable. That's why I stepped in and that's why I was summoned by the investigative magistrate of the BiH court concerning this, and I gave the same answers that I'm giving now. In principle, this could have taken place without any involvement of mine, but the duty officer wanted to check whether that Pecanac was really authorised to take over the prisoner, and the prison warden wanted to verify whether he really could hand the prisoner over, and the problem arose when Pecanac refused to sign. And then Savic chose to call me up and ask for advice what he should do so that he wouldn't be left hanging and be held accountable some day.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I appreciate that answer, Colonel. Does this document, first of all, record the events that you've just testified to about how Captain Pecanac came to pick up or retrieve Avdo Palic from the Vanikov Mlin prison? Is that what's essentially reflected in this document?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This document speaks about a correct procedure. Pecanac turned up at the gate of the military detention centre and introduced himself as an authorised official of the intelligence and security sector of the Main Staff and that he had arrived to take over Mr. Avdo Palic for subsequent treatment. Because the prison warden didn't know him personally, he wanted to make sure, since this was a member of the security service, called up the duty officer of the security department whose chief I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We've got that. I just want to know if it's talking about the same event that you're talking about, that this document relates to the that event, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What's talking about? I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Does this document with the signature of Pecanac and the signature of Savic relate to the event that you're testifying about?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does, but when I gave a statement to the investigative magistrate of the BiH court, I was shown another type of document that had a different title. It didn't -- it wasn't titled "Receipt". Actually, the title was inadequate, as if some objects had been handed over, not persons. That's the type of document I was shown in Bijeljina concerning the retrieval of Mr. Palic from military detention.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Mr. President, I'd like to tender this document before I forget to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before it will be received, I would like to put a question to the witness. Sir, you said Pecanac refused to sign this document. Why did he refuse to sign? Did he give you any reason for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, he didn't. And after talking to me, when the prison warden Milan Savic gave me Pecanac on the phone and wanted me to explain to him, and it was after midnight, so they had awoken me from deep sleep, and I asked Pecanac, "What's going on? Why don't you sign?" And then he started, "Well, you know ... " And then I got angry and said, "Okay, if you don't want to sign, get out of here and come back some other time." And he said, "Okay, okay." And that was the end of it. Why he initially didn't want to sign, well, you should ask him. Eventually he did so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. This document will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 7330 shall be assigned Exhibit Number P2182. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You referred a little bit earlier to Captain Pecanac as Pecko, and I think you indicated that you knew him. Can you tell us, if you know, what was his full name and what his position was in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His first --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: His full name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm certainly that his family name is Pecanac. I'm over 90 per cent sure that his first name is either Dragomir or Dragoljub. Those are very similar names. I think it's Dragomir. Whether back in 1995 he was a captain or major, I'm not sure. Even later than that, I was in the same position, we spoke and I saw him with the rank of major, but whether at this time he was a captain or not, I'm not sure, but anyway, it's the same person. I knew him from direct contacts that we had. He passed through Bijeljina travelling to Banja Luka. He needed fuel. Usually when somebody from the Main Staff was travelling toward Banja Luka, they would carry some mail that they would hand to us and then on the way back from Banja Luka toward the Main Staff they would again call on us and then possibly leave the mail that he had for us. So I did know him personally. But then I forgot what you wanted to -- there was another part of your question relating to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The question was what was his position in 1995? He was in the Main Staff. What position was he in?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was with the Main Staff in the security and intelligence administration. I am not sure, because he wasn't my subordinate, nor was he superior to me along the chain of command. I believe that for a while he was outside the security and intelligence administration -- or, rather, he may have been on an intelligence assignment in some sub-centre not far from Sarajevo, but that's only a hazy recollection. Anyway, all the time he was a member of the security and intelligence service. Which position he held at any point in time, I cannot say for certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And he was in a position in the security and intelligence administration of the Main Staff when you spoke to him on what appears to be the 5th of September of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer this question with full certainty. Whether he was a member of the security and intelligence administration or maybe detached somewhere. But at any rate, he was a member of the intelligence and security service, and he had the status of an authorised official for these tasks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You said - sorry for interrupting you - he was a member of the intelligence and security service. Which intelligence and security service, that one of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The intelligence and security service that -- yes, it did belong to the Main Staff, but in principle the intelligence and security service of the VRS as a whole is a parallel line --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I put a clear question to you. On page 19, lines 4 and 5, you said he was with the Main Staff in the security and intelligence administration. Later you said, "I cannot answer this question with full certainty." Then you said the -- "He was a member of the security and intelligence -- a member of the intelligence and security service," but you didn't say which unit. That one of the Main Staff or of another unit of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I answered with some uncertainty, because I did know people by name, but the exact designation of their establishment position was something didn't know, except for General Tolimir, that he was chief of the intelligence and security sector; and that Naval Captain Beara was chief of the security administration; and that Colonel Salapura was chief of the intelligence administration of the intelligence and security sector. There were others who came and went, among them Pecanac. What exactly his position was, whether he was a member of the security department or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry, again and again you were asked about his position in 1995. Was he a member of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You gave this answer already. He was with the Main Staff in the security and intelligence administration. That was your answer, and why -- do you stand by that? Do you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vanderpuye, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Colonel, you said you were called before a commission concerning the disappearance or the fate of Avdo Palic. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you remember what you told them about Pecanac's position in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember roughly. Not every word though. I do remember the essence of what I told them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you remember telling them that he was a security officer in the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what I was saying a minute ago, answering the question of the Presiding Judge. That's the terminology. I don't know what kind of interpretation you're receiving and how familiar you are with the establishment structure and the chart of individual positions. I don't remember whether he was a desk officer or a junior desk officer or something else, but certainly he was on the payroll of the intelligence and security sector, and in our army they -- these are often called "security guys [Realtime transcript read in error "guards"]" colloquially. He's a security guy.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Security guy or security guard?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Guy, interpreter's remark, g-u-y.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's an unpopular phrase. It's sort of slang, army slang, if you want. It's short for -- instead of security officer, they just say security guy. To cut things short, Pecanac was a security officer belonging to the sector for security and intelligence of the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Finally, we got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. I don't have any questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This concludes your examination-in-chief; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It does, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, now you may commence your cross-examination. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I wish peace unto this house, and may this hearing be concluding in keeping with God's will and not my own. I'd like to welcome the witness and wish him a pleasant stay with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Todorovic, during the past two days you were frequently asked about some facts, but I'd rather move on to something else which may you find -- you may find easier to answer. Let's look at your statement, which is 1D734. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, you indicated earlier that you would tender the statement of Mr. Todorovic, but you didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Ah, thank you for reminding me, and if it's not too late, I would offer it into evidence at this time. Mr. President, it's 1D733.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit Number P2183. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The document is now on the screen, P2183. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In your interview, you said that when the war broke out, you were at the Command Staff Academy in Belgrade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was in 1991, on the 20th of June. That is when the break-up of Yugoslavia turned violent with the conflict breaking out in Slovenia, and at that point in time I was at the military staff academy in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic. Nothing begins on its own and of itself. Can you tell us how the break-up of Yugoslavia began in Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you have asked this question to quite a lot of witnesses. I would like to know the purpose of putting these questions to a witness like Mr. Todorovic. That was not part of the examination-in-chief, and we have heard a lot of evidence about that, but which purpose -- what purpose do you think such a question could have in light of the indictment?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. In the interview that was just admitted, at page number 3, line 1, the witness says that in 1991, when the break-up began, he said: "In 1991, in July, when the break-up began, I did not return to Slovenia, because on the 26th of June, Slovenia," et cetera, et cetera. And this is where we stopped. I would like to ask that the witness be allowed to finish, because later on he was constantly being questioned as to whether he was assigned to the VRS, and in this interview we can see why it was impossible for him to go back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was just informed by the registrar that we have two different statements or interviews in front of us. One is 1D733 that was tendered by the Prosecution and received as P2183. Now we have on the screen 1D74 -- 734. It's a different one. That was my mistake. I was not aware of that. Just to clarify for the record. Do we have page number 3 of the document on the screen? We should have it, please. Mr. Tolimir, I need the reference for the English text.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We need 1D733, page 3, line 1. 1D733, page 3, line 1. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I assume you are referring to the B/C/S version, and now, please, the reference in English. And for the record, this is P2183.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in English it's page 3, the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I provide an answer to the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to ask Mr. Tolimir to repeat his question in relation to the text in front of us.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The question is this: Mr. Todorovic, can you explain to the Chamber why, after you completed the Command Staff Academy in Belgrade, you could not and did not return to your position in Slovenia where you had come from.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall the date as the 28th of June, 1991. That is two days following the declaration of independence and the beginning of an armed attack on the units and facilities of the JNA in Slovenia. As a student of the General Staff school, I decided to go to Maribor in my own vehicle to see what was going on with my family, my wife and younger daughter, because my older daughter had already been in Belgrade, at university. I arrived at the Slovenian border whereupon the Slovenia police refused to let me in because I had Belgrade registration plates on the car. Knowing the area well, I turned back and took a side road through the fields to get into Slovenia. Having served in Slovenia for some time, I used side roads to eventually reach the apartment where my family was. Within a short time, perhaps half an hour, since there was no time to arrange or argue anything, I basically told or ordered my family to pack the basic things they could fit in a bag and to leave for Belgrade. We were supposed to leave Maribor for our hometown of Bijeljina, actually, because both my wife and I hail from there. It was my intention to get them out of the combat area or the war-affected area and to accommodate them with my family or my wife's family, not taking into account that eventually it would still over into Bosnia. I didn't consider my employment or my position there, because as an active-duty officer I was prepared to go where assigned by the needs of service. Indeed, this is how things developed. My wife and daughter packed, and we took a few bags, locked the apartment, and left one key with our next-door neighbour. We used the same side roads to go back and exit Slovenia. We crossed Croatia in order to reach Bijeljina where I left my wife and daughter and returned to the school in Belgrade the same day in the evening. Let me say this as well: While I was driving through Slovenia, my car radio was on, and one could hear the news repeatedly of how the situation was very dangerous and complex and that the population was warned not to go outdoors. They were told to stay protected inside should there be any shelling or bombing. They were also advised on the most secure places within their own homes. As I was approaching Maribor, the news was that bombarders were -- bombers were up and that there was no one out in the street. That propaganda was so strong, trying to draw a picture of some insidious underhanded approach taken by the JNA which, in fact, did not exist. En route to Maribor, I was accompanied by a schoolmate whose family was also in Maribor. We reached Maribor together, and I dropped him off in front of his building. We arranged to go back together. However, he called me and said, "I'll return later, and you just go about your own business." Unfortunately, he stayed for over a month. He couldn't get out any more, because his movement was restricted. He didn't even attend the closing part or ceremony of the course. It also included another colleague from Vrhnika. There were also not present because the security organs prevented their exit from Slovenia. They arrived subsequently, but unfortunately could not attend the diploma award ceremony. That would be put in briefest possible terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: After Slovenia declared its independence on the 26th of June, two days later there was an attack on the JNA in Slovenia; is that correct? And can you tell us why the JNA was attacked in the former Yugoslav Republic of Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think you understood me. I said two days later, on the 28th of June. I remember that day, because it is an Orthodox holiday, and on that day I travelled to Slovenia to get my family, and I was discussing the news I could hear in the car while travelling. I have no direct knowledge of how things developed and what barracks were attacked. I have information from my colleagues and friends who served in Slovenia as I did. They talked about individuals, but politics is a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us how the units you served with in Slovenia came under attack, and did they remain there or were they driven out?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the garrisons were blocked. Town and city authorities were ordered to turn off electricity and water supply so as to render their stay there impossible. They were trying to make them surrender to the Slovenian Territorial Defence, which on the 26th of June became the official arm -- army of the Republic of Yugoslavia -- of Slovenia. Those sieges took quite some time, but the officers in the garrisons tried to cope with it as best they could and find different solutions to solve their problems. Finally, it was arranged with the political authorities in Slovenia that those units north of Ljubljana could leave Slovenia in an organised manner in order to move to some other garrisons. This was done, indeed. I know, for example, of the units from the Maribor general area where I served. I know where they left specifically. I can't speak exactly of the other units. My former brigade where I used to be in Slovenska Bistrica was moved to Gornji Milanovac in Serbia, somewhere in western Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, before you continue this line of questions, I would like to ask you again what is the purpose of putting questions about the secession of Slovenia and the impact on the VRS or the JNA at that time. We are -- in this case, we are not dealing with the conflict which started in 1991 and then went through 1992. We are discussing about 1995. In my view, it is a waste of time to put questions to that, and we have now used quite a lot of time with, in my view, irrelevant questions and answers. Please focus on the facts Mr. Todorovic can provide you with as knowledge. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. At page 4 of this interview, in lines 7 and 8, the Prosecutor asked Mr. Todorovic this: "We know you were in the JNA and that you were temporarily assigned to Bosnia, to a position in the VRS." One would conclude that Mr. Todorovic was sent to Bosnia directly without every mentioning that his former country fell apart and that he had to take his family out of the apartment they lived in. This all takes on a completely different connotation unless cleared up. This witness did not arrive in Bosnia because he was sent there by the VJ. He came their voluntarily. That is why I wanted to put these questions, because it is imputed here upon the Army of Yugoslavia that it was the VJ who sent officers to serve in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Where do I find this relevant part in the English version? Is it on the screen?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, it's on the screen, line 18 and 19. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. If you put questions to that. That was also raised in examination-in-chief, but the kind of questions was quite different. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, tell the Trial Chamber, had there not been the war in Slovenia, would you have returned to your service in Maribor from where you were sent to your training at the Command Staff Academy? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I certainly would have returned. I'm not sure whether it -- I spoke about that to the Prosecutor or Mr. Tomasz who examined me in February, but even now, after all this time, if I could meet the administrative criteria, one of which is citizenship, I would prefer returning to Slovenia to live there, because the best years of my life, from when I was 19 till the age of 42, I spent in Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic. I understand that you feel the need to speak about it, but my time is limited, and I have to ask all the questions I want to ask within a given time. What happened to the officers who served with you or were -- attended the same training and they were Slovenians? Were they able to remain members of the units of the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of us, and I'm speaking about my generation back in 1991, were sent where we wanted to go. There was no one Slovenian in my class. There were some Croats and Macedonians, some Albanians, Bosnians, and Serbs from Serbia, but most people were sent to serve in their own republic or -- I would have to recall it all. Maybe if somebody was married to a woman from Belgrade who had an appointment there, then probably they would be appointed to serve in Belgrade because they had a place to live even though he was not a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please give us a short answer. Since you served in the Army of Yugoslavia during the war in Slovenia and Croatia and later, did Slovenian officers of the JNA stay in the garrisons in Serbia where they served even after the war?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, most of them did. In the security administration, there was a lieutenant-colonel who was Slovenian, later was promoted to the rank of colonel, and he retired from the Army of Yugoslavia. Well, now it's the Army Of Serbia. But some of them went to their own country.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. That was going to be my following question. So those who wanted to stay, were able to stay, and those who wanted to leave, were able to leave?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I said already.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us whether officers from Bosnia-Herzegovina such as you because you were from Bijeljina were able to go to Bosnia-Herzegovina after the break-up of Yugoslavia and the secession of Bosnia-Herzegovina from Yugoslavia? Thank you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What period are you referring to, after 1995 or right after the beginning of the break-up of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the officers who hailed from Bosnia-Herzegovina after the secession of that republic from Yugoslavia, were they able to go to their own republic? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were able to go, and they were not a priori obliged to go there. Not everybody who hailed from there was automatically sent there. So there were two elements that were required: The will of the person in question and the needs of the service. I worked in the security administration of the VJ and one officer hailed from Foca. He never went there, not even to visit his family during that period, let alone to serve there. So it was not mandatory. Attempts -- efforts were made to reconcile the needs of the service and the origin of the person.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, first, you should pause between question and answer as you're using the same language. It's impossible for the interpreters to follow. The second is we need the first break now. We adjourn and resume at 11.00, and then you may continue your questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir. Please continue, and try to use your time in the most sufficient way, and try not to deal with matters which are irrelevant for this case. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I apologise, but very different things have been established with regard to adjudicated facts that we do not acknowledge. Here we have before us an officer who has first-hand experience with this break-up. Not only him but his family too. And I do not accept the adjudicated facts about the break-up of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, when I ask you a question, please watch the screen in front of you, and once the cursor stops moving, then start your answer, and please answer briefly. If possible, give a yes or no answer, because otherwise I won't be able to ask all my questions. Here's my following question: Did the Muslim personnel in the JNA who did not accept the secession of Slovenia, Croatia, and Bosnia-Herzegovina, were they able to remain in their officers' position in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia even after the secession of the respective republics of Yugoslavia? Thank you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were able to, and I know some examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell us, do you know when the Muslim part, the so-called Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, separated itself from the Republika Srpska and when did Bosnia-Herzegovina break up?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure about the date. I know that the 9th of January is mentioned as the day of statehood in Republika Srpska. I cannot speak about other dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know what the -- what the day of statehood of Bosnia-Herzegovina is and when Bosnia-Herzegovina was recognised as a country by certain countries, members of the European Union? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that two dates are observed, the 29th of November. That is the -- or, rather, the 26th of November. That's the old day of statehood. On that day the second session of AVNOJ took place. And then there's another date, the 2nd of March or April. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you ever heard that Bosnia-Herzegovina was recognised by some EU members and NATO members on the 6th of April, as you said?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't really say the 6th of April, but I did say it was some date in March or April.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether Slovenia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Croatia were rewarded for seceding from Yugoslavia by their international recognition?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 4, lines 8 and 9, the Prosecutor asked you whether you were sent to -- deployed to Bosnia to perform duty in VRS. So now tell me, the officers who hailed from Bosnia-Herzegovina, did they have a status before the break-up in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did every --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir and Mr. Todorovic, please pause between question and answer and the next question. Carry on, please, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, please tell us, did every member of the former SFRY provide money for their personnel in the federal structures, and were those funds used for paying out salaries, social contributions, et cetera, for members of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't quite understand. Are you referring to the period until the secession or after?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Until the secession. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the secession there were no financial funds broken down by the republics for the needs of the Yugoslav People's Army. There was a federal level at which all this funding was taken care of, including salaries, housing, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell us if all republics, members of Yugoslavia, were obliged to contribute money from their budgets to the federal budget. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not an economist, so I cannot provide a precise answer, but part of the federal budget was fed from the republican budgets.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that the Republika Srpska - I'm referring to the republic, not the army - after the beginning of combat activities reached an agreement with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia that it was supposed to contribute to the budget of Yugoslavia, whereas Yugoslavia would pay out the salaries of the officers serving in the RS.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that there was such an agreement, because all members who were temporarily deployed to the VRS received their salaries and other benefits from the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know, Mr. Todorovic, that based on this agreement between the RS and the FRY, that is Serbia, the VRS reached an agreement with the JNA to accommodate five to six officers who were supposed to be in charge of personnel affairs concerning its members who took part in the war? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This small part of the personnel was called the 30th Personnel Centre. There was the 30th and there was the 40th. As far as I know, the 30th was in charge for the VRS, whereas the 40th was in charge of the Army of the Republic of the Serb Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please wait.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic. Please answer this question if you know: Did the funds of the health insurance or the medical insurance that were paid in for army members even before the war were acquired rights of members of the JNA and members of their family who were entitled to receive medical treatment in medical facilities of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know about that, and that was indeed made use of. Even now retired members of the former JNA who are in the territory of the RS can receive medical treatment in medical facilities of the Republic of Serbia based on their acquired rights and their years of service, which the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia acknowledged as the accessory of the former SFRY, and so did the Republic of Serbia later.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that the agreements reached between the former Yugoslav republics, including those that seceded, acknowledge the acquired rights of former -- the acquired rights of people who worked in Yugoslavia, including --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please repeat the end of his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Since you are putting your questions in a very fast manner, the interpreters didn't get and catch the last part of your question. Please repeat it and slow down a bit.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, do you know that after the secession, even the former Yugoslav republics through their agreement on secession represented the obligation to provide social rights and social welfare to all citizens who could transfer these rights to the republic where they now live? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know about this. And it has functioned for awhile with Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, and toward the end of last year, an international agreement was signed with Slovenia, and the disbursement of pensions and other benefits to inhabitants of Serbia began recently, those who acquired some rights based on living in those republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic. Please tell us, did the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia or Serbia ever deny their acquired rights to any citizen who lived in former Yugoslavia, or did they continue to pay salaries to them and housing, et cetera, irrespective of who -- which army they joined? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that too. Civilians were paid continuously, and members of the former JNA received their salaries and other benefits up to the moment that they filed an application to -- for termination of service in the JNA, but tenancy rights were not denied them, nor the rights that they had with regard to any real estate in Serbia. I know some examples of swapping apartments between members of the former JNA who lived in Slovenia. I know more about Slovenia, because I lived there for quite a while and worked there. So they swapped apartments, and the state accepted that and it was all legal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic. Please tell us, do you know whether the apartments of army members in the secessionist republics of Slovenia, Croatia, and Bosnia-Herzegovina were taken away by force and was that done in the same way in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia too? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can use my own example. My apartment in Maribor was assigned to a member of the army of Slovenia or some other Slovenian citizen. However, when I retired, based on all the rights acquired, I was given an apartment in Belgrade. I know of a number of colleagues who could not exercise their right to have those apartments returned to them, be it for the purpose of residing in it or exchanging it for another, and this applied to all the former republics, that is to say, the three you mentioned, Slovenia, Croatia, and Bosnia. I don't have much information about Macedonia. I don't know anything about the interstate agreements.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic. Let's look at page 5 of your statement, lines 1 through 8.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's page 6 in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I will refer you to the right lines, and you can explain. You say that you worked in Belgrade in the security administration, and you and Mr. Lugonja were there as members of the VRS, given the fact that you both hailed from Bosnia and Herzegovina before you joined the East Bosnia Corps. Can you explain this period to the Chamber and tell them of the existence of that one office which took care of VRS personnel who happened to be in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew Marko Lugonja from the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. We were at the same level, but he was with the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Once he concluded his education in Belgrade, in the operations school, he was assigned to the security administration of the army of the FRY where I happened to be, having returned from the war in Republika Srpska. We were next-door colleagues, and in 1998, based on the same principle that was applied in 1993, when I was asked by General Tolimir to respond to their call and take part temporarily in the formation of the VRS, General Lugonja asked me to accompany him to the VRS, because he was to be appointed the chief of security of the Main Staff of the VRS in peacetime, since it was 1998. I gave it some thought, and I accepted for the same reasons I did in 1993. Therefore I did respond and was temporarily assigned to the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Todorovic, since you returned to the VRS after the war, we need to look at page 4 of your interview, lines 21 to 24. In those lines, if you can see then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please give us the reference in the English text.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 6 in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which line?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, to save time, I will simply recount what you stated, and then I will have a question for you. Here you describe that on the 16th of November, 1993, until February 1997, you were chief of the intelligence and security administration, and then between 1998 and 2002, you were at the position specified, whereupon you were retired. You mentioned how you worked in the Weapons Reduction Commission, and you how you attended courses in Oberammergau in Germany and you also were present in Vienna when the agreement was implemented. Let's look at 65 ter 05415 [as interpreted] and tell us whether it was based on this agreement that you exercised your duties as control -- weapons inspector as part of the commission for weapon control.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the number of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, could you please repeat the number of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 05714. It is on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We see a document of the Main Staff, the date is the 31st of March and it's titled "Report on Negotiations and the Agreement of Regional Stabilisation". It mentions that between the 18th and 29th of March there were negotiations in Vienna when this agreement was reached. In seven items specified below, among others we see in item 1 "Agreement on subregional arms control". Was it based on this agreement reached in Vienna that you were assigned to the commission for reduction and arms control?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was based on this agreement that I was sent to Oberammergau to attend short -- a short training. I wanted to say that in 1998, the reduction process had basically been completed, and the commissions of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croatia, and Serbia jointly toured all military locations in those locations, controlling the declared as opposed to factual situation with the armaments and whether the signatories abided by the provisions of the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we please have page 2 in e-court so that we could see what the limits were to which you had to reduce the weapons in the respective republics. We see items (a) to (e) with the respective entities and the minimum of heavy weaponry retained after reduction. Look at page 2. Was it your job to have the number of weapons in the respective entities brought down to the level specified?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the task of the commission. In 1998, when I appeared in the VRS for the second time, our primary task was to control the whereabouts of those weapons and whether those locations had been declared and whether there were any deviations or violations of the agreement. By 1998, the figures were indeed brought down to these levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic. Let's look at the last page of the document so as to see the signature block. It was signed by a representative of the RS, and at that time it was Major-General Zdravko Tolimir, assistant commander. This document that Mr. Todorovic abided by in the course of his work is something that I seek to tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I don't quite understand the purpose of tendering this document from 1996, if I'm not mistaken. Could you please explain that. If I'm not mistaken, this is relating to a time period after the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I quoted from page 4 of the interview before referring to this document. It was lines 21 through 30 where the witness addressed this topic when discussing it with the investigators. This was the basis for the agreement to be admitted just so that we could understand what mechanisms were used to reduce the number of weapons. This is part of the general activities of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This document will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 5714 shall be assigned Exhibit Number D219. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Let us look at page 6 of the interview, lines 30 to 34 in the Serbian. It is P2183. In the English version, it's the next page, page 7. Apologies. In English, it is page 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, yesterday in examination-in-chief, you were asked by Mr. Vanderpuye how you arrived in Yugoslavia, and you discussed how I came to see General Dimitrijevic when we met for the first time. What you said about 1993, does it have to do with the encounter we had at the security administration of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does. I don't know whether it was in May or June, but around mid-1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was there any basis in the laws and agreements between the FRY and the RS on which I could look for personnel that was in the FRY to try and ask them to join the RS army voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe we touched upon that in a previous question. I said that voluntariness was applied, and the other criterion was the needs of the service, and I did specify that some colleagues of mine refused for their own personal reasons. I said that a colleague from Foca never came back to Republika Srpska, not even to visit his family, let alone to serve there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us go to page 10, lines 11 through 16. I will quote once we see them. It's page 11 in the English, the last paragraph. Here you say that the other professional officers in your department, such as Dragan Tomic and those who were not from the reserve staff, were on the payroll of the VJ. Was it only through the payroll and accountancy done by the 30th Personnel Centre that they received their salaries from the RS funds, or did they receive their salary directly from the VJ?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I specified that the only member of the security department headed by me from the reserve force was Dragan Tomic. He was a reserve officer of the VRS, and his name was not on any payroll lists of the Army of Yugoslavia. The other subordinates of mine in the intelligence and security department of the East Bosnia Corps were active-duty members of the Army of Yugoslavia or of the VRS, and their names can be found on all payroll lists that existed in the 30th Personnel Centre of the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic. At page 10, starting with line 25, and then at page 11, you mention Mr. Mitrovic. You also do that on page 12. Actually, it's page 12 in the English. You mentioned Ljubo Mitrovic as the president of the exchange commission. Can you tell us whether Ljubo Mitrovic was subordinated to you, or did you only provide advice and guidelines to him since you were in personal contact and you knew him from earlier on when he served with the Semberija Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only provided guidelines, and I clarified issues that weren't necessarily clear to him. He was not my subordinate directly. In the part you referred to, I was trying to explain that he asked to be in the security and intelligence department of the East Bosnia Corps on paper so that no one could transfer him for various reasons. That is why Mr. Mitrovic, on paper, had his office seat in the intelligence and security department of the East Bosnia Corps. His other function was -- or, actually, the president of the exchange commission was subordinated to the commander of the East Bosnia Corps. I explain in the interview that he had a separate office outside the corps command, at the other end of town. He had his own secretary and phone line and the fax machine. He had a separate vehicle and could work autonomously and independently when exercising his duties as the president of the exchange commission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: At this point in time I would like to put a question to clarify. You said, sir, on page 43, lines 12 through 15, and I quote: "The other subordinates of mine in the intelligence and security department of the East Bosnia Corps were active-duty members of the Army of Yugoslavia or the VRS." Can you tell me to which time period you are referring when you give this information. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was referring to the wartime period. In other words, 1993 through 1997. And then in 1998 through 2000, it was a bit different. It was a combination of factors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Mr. Todorovic, for the transcript, just tell us loud and clear, without any explanations, who was Ljubo Mitrovic subordinated to? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the East Bosnia Corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic. Let us now take a look at page 12 where on lines 1 through 7, and that will be page 13 in the English, you talk about reconnaissance units, and you mention proposals that you submitted to the commander in relation to those units. I will read out from line 3 of your statement, and I quote: "All units, including the military police, had reconnaissance units that were subordinated to the commander -- or, rather, to the Chief of Staff, and in the case of the police and their reconnaissance units, I propose their use in the most effective way. The commander usually accepted and agreed to my proposals, but he did not have to." Bearing this in mind, for the needs of the transcript could you please tell us whether military police units and the reconnaissance units that you provided professional guidance to, were they under your command or the under the commands of their officers.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it's very clear from what I said here that their commander was the corps commander and I, as a professional, and along the professional chain of command actually proposed their employment in the most effective manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can we please take a look now at P1297 in e-court, and let us see what the legal provisions are for the use of those. Thank you. Thank you. We see before us the service regulations for the military police. Let us now take a look at page 6 of this document, paragraph 2. Thank you. Could we please just move the text a bit so that the witness can see it. Thank you. We see what this -- these service regulations actually provide for, and I will read this out for you. Now we see it in the English version as well. The second half of the first paragraph says that the regulations are based on the provisions of the federal laws and other federal regulations. My question for you is this: In units of the VRS during the war, did you apply these rules from the Army of Yugoslavia in keeping with the regulations that were in force at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. We did apply the rules of service of the Yugoslav Army, including the one that we have before us, and it frequently occurred that in a document we would make a reference to that. We would say based on the rules of service of the military police, for instance, of the Yugoslav Army taken over by the VRS.
