So we would make that the reference in order to actually point to the regulation or rule that was referred to there. This had to do with various services, including the security organ, and it was -- they were used up until the end of the war, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In view of what you've just said, would you look at paragraph 2 here, and I'd like to ask you this: Did these regulations provide a basis for the command and control of the military police within the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. That's what I said in reply to your previous question already.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now please take a look at the first sentence of paragraph 3, and I will read it out. "The regulations are intended for the following: Members of the armed police for their unified approach when executing the tasks from their jurisdiction." Now, my question is this: As an organ who commanded the military police, would you please tell me this reference here to a unified approach, what exactly does that mean? Does that mean that a military policeman in Belgrade, in Banja Luka, in Drvar or anywhere would have to abide by it.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, exactly as you stated there, these regulations were in fact drafted in order for a unified approach to be applied and not every individual taking his own decisions as they please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We have a problem with the transcript because you were overlapping again. I can't see where the answer started. Now it's corrected. Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, you quoted from this document but in a very different way of that part we see in the English translation. Perhaps it is a translation issue, but if you read a text into the transcript, it should be really a serious quotation. I see a different part in the -- oh, yes, I see. You were reading from paragraph 3. I heard from paragraph 2. Thank you very much. Now I see it. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, would you please explain here whether in this unified approach that was something that was taught in schools, written down in laws, was the fundamental underlying principle that the military police should be commanded by the commander and not anyone else and that the military police did not have to have a commander, komandir, who would actually tell them what to do at every single step, because they had actually learned that principle during their schooling?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the course of their training, the training of the military police; and this included military police, plain military police as well as their commanders, they had to learn their duties and obligations and rights, including the right to take into custody, apply force if necessary, ask for IDs, and so on. So all those rights that fall within the jurisdiction of the military police. They learned that during their training.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, based on your experience, and you've told us that you served in Slovenia, in Serbia, in Bijeljina, and so on, would a military policeman have to apply exactly the same approach and take the same action in any of those places, as far as your experience is concerned, if, for instance, he approached a military person, a soldier, and asked for his ID?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly. They would have to abide by the same rules and follow exactly the same procedure when asking for IDs, and there was no limit on which rank they could actually intercept, stop, and ask for their IDs. In other words, a staff sergeant could ask for an ID from -- of a major, and this applied anywhere, whether Belgrade or Skopje or anywhere in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now please show the witness page 7. I'd like him to take a look at it and then I will have a question for the witness. And that will be chapter 1. Perhaps you already have it there. "General provisions." Can we show it in English, please? Yes. Now we have it in the English version. I will only read out the first sentence from paragraph 1. I quote: "The military police are composed of specially trained and equipped unites of the armed forces which perform certain duties, as follows: Security for the needs -- for the needs of the armed forces, protection of people and property, safety and military traffic, maintenance of soldierly order and discipline and uncovering crimes and perpetrators," and so on. Now, Mr. Todorovic, could you please tell the Chamber did every member of the military police undergo special training in order to be able to carry out the duties as described here?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Commanding officers, who were assigned to military police units after undergoing general training, more often than not, that would be infantry or mechanised training. They would then be sent to Pancevo to the special military security school where staff were trained for the needs of the military police, whereas soldiers who were members of the military police were -- underwent training within the unit where they were assigned up until the moment when they were reassigned to a unit where they would serve, where they would undergo specialised training depending on what kind of tasks they had to deal with in that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic. Yesterday in the course of the examination-in-chief you were asked whether you had commanded military police who provided -- who guarded the prisoners in Batkovic. Now, let us take a look at page 9 of this document before us, at paragraph 12, and see what we have there. That's chapter 2, and it says "Command and control of the military police." And that will be on page 10 in the English version. Now we have it in English as well. And we see that it says as follows: "The officer in charge of the military unit and institution within whose establishment the military police unit is placed or to which it is attached commands and controls the military police." Now, pursuant to this, would you please tell me who it was who commanded, who was the commander of the military police at the collection centre in Batkovic and within whose establishment were they?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the military collection centre in Batkovic, as I explained yesterday, there were some 20 to 25 military police - in other words, a Military Police Platoon - and they were part of the military police battalion of the East Bosnia Corps. They were resubordinated -- or, rather, attached to the collection centre, and the commanding officer of that platoon was in daily communication to discuss any difficulties or problems they were facing with the warden of the collection centre. However, if he needed clothes, uniforms, equipment, and so on, or if he needed to replace personnel, then he would address these issues to his direct commander, which was the battalion commander, the military police battalion commander. In other words, that platoon was temporarily assigned to the collection centre in order to carry out the guard duties there, and it was taken from under the battalion command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic. Would you tell the Trial Chamber who was the commanding officer of the military police battalion, and in what -- to what unit did he or they belong?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military police battalion was under the command of the commander of the military police, Captain Vulin, later Major Vulin, and it was -- it had under it the structure of the battalion, and his commander was the commander of the East Bosnia Corps, General Simic Novica.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not sure of the first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the name of this man, General Simic. What was his first name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Novica Simic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, let us look at item 13, what it says about the powers of the security organ with regard to the military police in general. It says the military police is controlled along professional lines by the commander of the unit or facility to which the military police unit belongs or to which it is attached. Here's my question to you. Did you have the right to exert professional control over the military police unit of the East Bosnia Corps given your position in the security service?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was both my right and my duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please explain the Trial Chamber how you went about it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I conducted frequent inspection and audits. If I observed some shortcomings in the activities of the military police, I would point that out to the commander, and I would set deadlines and define tasks for the rectification of those shortcomings, and I would also acquaint the corps commander for him to be up-to-date, and in accordance -- or depending on need, I would propose measures for him to take. For example, disciplinary measures or even the opposite; if somebody did a very good job, that person should be -- should receive some incentives.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic, now please take a look at Article 2, paragraph 2, quote for the transcript: "In carrying out tasks from the remit of the military police, based on need and the decision of the military officer in charge, the following can -- can engage in co-ordinated action with the military police," and so on. Here's my question: Did you have any powers with regard to units that are deployed to join other units, to act in co-ordinated action with them, or was it somebody else? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You were referring to Article 2 in your question, but I can't see any such article here on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Todorovic. I misquoted. I quoted from item 1, but we see Chapter II. I'm going to quote from paragraph 3, but do answer my question that I asked about item 2 of general provisions?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please display the English version too. It's on page 8 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now you can see paragraph 2 of item 2. So that military police units can be part of co-ordinated action. So who has authority over them in such a case?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the commander who takes the decision on co-ordinated action when he decides about combat activities, be it defence, attack or any other activity. In that case, he determines who has the main role. If the military police unit acts in co-ordination with another unit, then that other unit would mostly probably be a reconnaissance unit because they have trained in a very similar manner. So the attached part that acts in co-ordination must be instructed or trained, and its training will be conducted by the commander of the military police unit because he is basically responsible for that task. Of course if he needs professional assistance, he will contact the chief of the security organ so that he may contribute to that training.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic. I asked you this because yesterday you were asked whether the military police unit in Zvornik took part in combat as it was presented by Mr. Pandurevic in his report of 16 July 1995. Please tell us if you remember that. Did the military police unit, once it arrived in the zone of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade was under the authority of the commander of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because the military police unit, which was part of the military police battalion that was deployed to Zvornik was only sent there to carry out a specific task, namely to accept some of the members of the BH Army taken prisoner and to conduct them to the Batkovic collection centre. That's a task he received from the battalion commander, and I only relayed it to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now the transcript stopped. Please now put the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic. Do explain the following: If it had been the way Pandurevic stated in his report, if they had fought as a unit of the Zvornik Brigade, who would have had authority over them?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there had been a need to use the military police unit in such a way, I mean from the East Bosnia Corps, in principle, the Main Staff through you or the operative organ should have issued an order to the effect that the command of the East Bosnia Corps should deploy a unit to act in co-ordination with part of the military police to carry out the combat mission given to the commander of the Zvornik Brigade. Since that was not the case, that is, the commander of the battalion of the East Bosnia Corps did not receive such a task, he was not to take part in the performance of any combat mission, and I believe he wasn't. In that scenario, when the commander of the military police from the East Bosnia Corps reported to the Zvornik Brigade that he had arrived with so-and-so many men, equipment and the like, and placing himself under that commander's command for a certain period, he should have received a specific task from that commander, and the commander of the Zvornik Brigade should have made sure that that unit was indeed capable of carrying out that mission. I hope I've been able to answer your question as it was intended.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic, you did, but state clearly for the transcript. If they had fought as part of the Zvornik Brigade as it was reported, would the one in charge of combat activities in the zone of responsibility of the brigade have been responsible for that or the command of the East Bosnia Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please start over with his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, you started too early. We don't have it on the record. Please repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not so used to this. I apologise. Of course, everything that's happening in the zone of responsibility of a unit, here specifically the Zvornik Brigade, is in the responsibility of the commander of the Zvornik Brigade, and if he were to decide to use these military police forces, as has been stated, he should have given them a specific task and after that received a report of what has been done. After that, he could thank them and send them back to their original unit. So it's the commander of the Zvornik Brigade who is responsible for everything in the zone of responsibility of that brigade and not the commander of the military police battalion or the commander of the East Bosnia Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic. Let us take another look at page 9, command and control of the military police, and answer only the questions that I'm about to ask about paragraph 2 of item 13. You can see that second paragraph. Here's my question: Do officers of the security organ with regard to the military police have the same authority as the officers of the arms and services with regard to those arms and services, that is, only an advisory authority?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can provide an extensive answer. The chief of artillery proposes how the artillery should be used and the commander accepts or refuses, and the same goes for the commander of the military police, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I see that we have the document in e-court. I think it would be helpful to read into the record what it says specifically, because I don't see in the English translation of the document in the second paragraph under 13 the word "advisory" anywhere. So maybe either the witness can explain it, or we can have that read into the -- into the record so that it's clear what he's responding to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, would you please read the second paragraph of item 13 into the record. Then we will receive the correct translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "When controlling a military police unit, the officer in charge of the security organ from paragraph 1 of this item has the same rights and duties as the officers of the arms and services of military units and institutions in controlling the units of the arms and services." And the third paragraph elaborates that more specifically. Since the military police also has a traffic police component, which is a platoon or a company where it is the assistant commander for traffic who gets involved, which means that I as the security organ propose how the general component of the military police unit is to be used whereas the use of the traffic police component is something where the chief or, rather, the assistant for traffic police gets involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think that was enough. Mr. Tolimir should continue with his questioning.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Todorovic, with regard to the military police unit, does the chief of the traffic service have the same rights as you with regard to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please repeat the latter part of his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, could you please repeat the last part of the question, and I would like to ask the witness to wait until the transcript stops. It's very difficult, but as you are using the same language, it's absolutely necessary to pause. Mr. Tolimir, please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does, with regard to the traffic component of the military police, the chief of the traffic police have the same rights as the organ, security organ, of the corps command? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, which means that the traffic organ and the corps command, and in any other command, exercises professional control as well as training, equipping of that part of the military police whose duty it is to control traffic. He proposes its use during the performance of certain tasks, the same way as I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic. Does the same principle that the security organ only has the right to give professional direction, does this -- is this regulated in the rules of service of the security organs?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One of the tasks, I believe it's the fourth or the fifth task in the rules of service of the security organs, is the control of the military police activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's see D203, page 10 in Serbian and page 11 in English. We're interested in item 23 of the rules of service of the security organs in the armed forces, and this provision regulates the same matter of -- as the rules of the military police do. Thank you. We can see item 23 in both Serbian and English. It's item 23 of the rules of service of the security organs in the armed forces. I quote: "An officer of a security organ of a command unit, institution, or staff of the armed forces provides specialist management for a military police unit. He recommends the use of the military police unit to the senior officer of the command, unit, institution or staff, and he is responsible to him for the state of the activity of the unit." Now I'll continue to read the second paragraph: "In controlling the military police unit, the security organ officer under paragraph 1 of this item has the same rights and duties as officers of the arms and services of commands, units, institutions and staffs of the armed forces in controlling units of the arms and services of those commands, units, institutions or staffs." My question based on this is does the security organ have the right to command military police units, or does it only have the right to control them?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just wait a moment. No problem. Just wait a moment, and I would like to ask Mr. Tolimir to repeat the number of this document so that we have it clear on the record.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It is D203. The title is rules of service of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I just wanted to have the document number. Now, please, Mr. Todorovic, provide us with your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Item 23 is identical to the item we saw a moment ago in the rules of service of the military police. There shouldn't be any difference. The officer in charge of the security organ manages, supervises and controls, whereas command lies with the commander. Commands are issued by commanders, and chiefs and assistant commanders are in charge of checking whether the orders have been implemented correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic. Since you were at different positions in security organs at the level of brigade, corps, administration, and the Main Staff for a number of years, please explain to the Chamber what is a difference between command and control? Perhaps you can clarify that so as -- so as not to get confused by the two terms. Since my legal assistant tells me that "rukovodjenje" is translated as "control". So can you explain the difference between command, control, and managing?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Command or commanding is a method applied to directly manage certain units or institutions of the army of the -- of the FRY or any other army, including the -- the previous JNA. So there is a right to engage directly and make direct decisions on the activities of a unit, including personnel issues. In this way, the commander in question directly imposes his decisions on his subordinates. Control, as the second term, includes professional or specialist assistance to the commander. The commander, of course, cannot be specialised in all the areas, starting with the military police, the engineering corps, the nuclear defence units, et cetera. That is why he has his assistants -- assistants, to provide professional work and guidance, as well as training for those units and the way that they ought to be used. The third term used is "kontrola". As of the moment the commander issues a task, there is a process of control in place to oversee the implementation of those orders. If there is a need for correction of the order, then this is made based on the situation found and based on recommendations made by the professional or specialist organs. This can also be done if the commander himself realises that he had ordered something which cannot be implemented. Then he will amend his order, and he will be included personally so as to see that the task is correctly implemented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I ask you to repeat the three terms. You explained the three terms Mr. Tolimir was asking you about. Could you please repeat only the three terms without an explanation, because we have a translation issue here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Komandovanje," command; "Rukovodjenje," control; and "kontrola".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I dislike doing this [In English] The term "control" have to be translated in Serbian "kontrola". Directing, managing is something what is in Serbian "rukovodjenje". [Interpretation] We are discussing technical terms. However, we have repeated errors in the transcript. So as to avoid translating "kontrola" with "control," whereas the word "rukovodjenje" is constantly being translated as "kontrola."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: It's been a long-standing practice of the CLSS to translate "rukovodjenje" and "komandovanje" as command and control, C2. It is standard NATO terminology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is true. We have dealt with this problem several times here in this trial, and we will not solve this problem today I'm sure, but we know what we have to do in future. I think it's time for the second break. We will resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, I see you on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'll be brief, and I will abide by what you said, that we definitely won't deal with the issue today. However, at page 62, lines 21 to 23, in the interpreter's note, this seems to be the crux of the problem, that when translating expert terms of the VRS and the VJ, corresponding NATO terminology is used, which is a completely differently structured military organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is your position. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just briefly, Mr. President. I don't really think this is a problem, and CLSS has worked this out a long time ago. When they say command and control, that is the correct English interpretation, and the term "control" in English includes managing and some of the other terms mentioned by Mr. Gajic. The term "kontrola" in Serbian doesn't and that's where the problem is, but if he looks at the term "control" in English as a broader managing term, then I think we're fine, and we're of course working with him on any documents where he thinks management might be a better word for control, but I don't really think it's a problem. We fundamentally agree with these things. It's just a -- it's just a word issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think it's nothing we have to judge about today. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence reserves the right to engage in experts should such problems persist who will deal with the issue, hopefully. Of course this will take a lot of time, but I believe things need to be cleared up so as to have everything in a uniform way, because expert terms are translated differently. I know there is no perfect solution, but when we are discussing technical terms, there must be standard practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. May I, before we continue with the cross-examination of the witness, ask the Defence if they will be in a position to respond to the urgent Prosecution motion for protective measures for the witness to come. We received this motion this morning, and I think it's really an urgent motion. We would be happy to receive your response as soon as possible orally in the courtroom. It's not necessary to do that now, but I would like -- kindly invite you to respond. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we could do this right away. We have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that. The Chamber will issue a decision as soon as possible. Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, we looked at item 23 concerning the officers of security organs and commands of institutions and units. In order to discuss the gist of the problem and the terms used, I believe we need to look at the following: Perhaps you can tell us what the scope of work of security organs is and whether NATO terminology could be applied. Let's look at page 5 in the B/C/S and 6 in the English version. We see the title, "The competence and tasks of security organs." And "The competence of security organs". We are still reading from the rules of service. "1. Security organs as specialist organs of commands, units, institutions and staffs of the armed forces, carry out documents of state security that are placed within their competence by the law and regulations issued pursuant to the law ..." Can different terminology be used when discussing laws and regulations we had to abide by as parts of the security structure?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It cannot be interpreted differently to what it says here. Unfortunately, I'm not familiar with any other terminology, because I had not had occasion to study similar laws and regulations on the work of units and services of other armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic. In the course of your work, could you deviate from the scope accorded to you based on the laws and regulations in order to discover and detect activities of the enemy solely based on the use of different terminology, or did you have to abide strictly by the word of the laws and regulations?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not deviate, and there was no need to. This is what I studied, and I had these rules in front of me, including the rules of work of security organs and the rules of work of the military police. All security organs and military police organs of East Bosnia Corps had the same rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we look at page 7 in English and 8 in Serbian. Could we see the -- yes, this side of this page 13. Let us look at sub-item (b). This is a very important issue. Actually, it is (d) "performing special administration services for military police units." And then (e) "operations that precede the initiation of criminal proceedings ..." What does it mean, "operation preceding initiation of criminal proceedings?"

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure we're looking at the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir referred to items (d) and (e). You can see the page where the clauses are located.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It has to do with the following: If there is -- there are reasons to suspect that a crime was committed in a unit of the army, security organs gather initial information. In further procedure, they can partially or in full engage members of the military police. In the military police battalions and military police companies, there used to be departments for criminal or investigative measures with the aim of documenting and preparing evidence. In that case, the security organ issues a specific task to the unit commander, the commander of the military unit, to act specifically. If it concerned stolen weapons, an on-site investigation had to be carried out, reports drafted and evidence secured so as to continue any criminal procedure with a view to identifying and sanctioning the perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic. When you look at item (e) which begins with the words "operations that precede the initiation of criminal proceedings," do investigative organs have the right in profession -- in the professional sense to direct the actions of the military police unit which was tasked with documenting and preserving evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In all serious offences, the security organ is duty-bound to inform a military court and in such cases an investigating judge is appointed. Whether he would be in charge of the pre-trial procedure depended on the gravity of crime. If the crime resulted in deaths, then it is obligatory that the investigating judge is in charge of documenting and securing evidence in investigation. In less serious crimes, he can authorise members of the military police to gather evidence and document its existence in order to prove that a crime was committed and to ensure that the perpetrators are identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic. We have just spoken about the investigative organs and their right to engage the organs of the military police to document a crime from item 7(e). I will now ask you to take a look at page 13 in English and page 11 in Serbian and tell us how the methods of the security organs can be applied to carry out tasks from items 6 and 7. We have just read out 7(e). Thank you. Thank you. Now we can see Chapter III in both languages. The second paragraph of item 26 reads -- or, rather, the first item reads: "Pursuant to his powers under the federal law ..." and I won't go on reading, so there must be a legal foundation. The second paragraph reads: "In carrying out duties and tasks under items 6 and 7(A) and (F) of these rules, JNA security organs may apply methods and means, and also measures and operations that deviate from the principle of the inviolability of secrecy of letters and other means of communications in accordance with regulation in paragraph 1 of this item." Can you explain to the Trial Chamber in which situations the security organs of the military police have the right to act to -- to act contrary to the law and use such methods and means?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are situations when intelligence is received that there are grounds to suspect that preparations are underway for the perpetration of a crime or when the perpetration is possible, given the circumstances. Based on this initial intelligence, the security organ drafts a note and proposes the choice of a certain -- certain method to collect concrete information to either confirm the suspicion or reject it. Only when the security organ receives approval from the competent authority to use the method in question which approval is granted for a certain period of time. For example, inspecting letters whose recipient is a person that is suspected to be in connection with some criminal offence, then the secrecy of private correspondence can be infringed upon from the 1st of May through the 15th of June, for example. So a deadline is set by which it must be established whether there are grounds for suspicion or not. The application of these methods require approval from the competent officer or commander in an army or, in some cases, approval from a court. With that, the approval of these institutions, the security organ had the right to do the following: Interview members of the armed forces, check their ID, check their personal information in various files such as birth registers and so on in order to avoid errors, and -- whereas all other methods required approval and a time-frame.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic. Please tell us, did the investigating judge --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please repeat the question. The interpreter didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The interpreter asked you to repeat your question because he didn't understand it, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I asked Mr. Todorovic if in case of serious criminal offences that are difficult to document, did the investigating judge entrust the security organs of the military police with conducting entire investigation in order to document these criminal offences such as, for example, theft of armaments, ammunition, or other criminal offences against the armed forces. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there have been such instances, several, and incidents of aggravated theft of weapons were treated for months or even years, and the security organs were authorised to try and reveal the perpetrators of these crimes and recover the stolen armaments, and that included inspections on the ground, checking the soldier and his relatives and the area where he hails from, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic. Let us go to page 5 in Serbian and page 6 in English. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Mindua has a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Witness. Just a very short question. This permission, this authorisation that was given to the security organ, was it given once and that was good for all the time, or was it case-per-case depending on the suspect and depending on the accused?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was specific for each incident on a case-by-case basis, and it was always specified what is expected as -- as the result of the application of this method of work. So it wasn't just arbitrary and all-encompassing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Mindua.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, we are in a position here to have to stress often that security organs are professional organs. So take a look at item 5, which says the following -- or, rather, item 1: "Security organs, as specialist organs of commands, units, institutions and staffs of the armed forces, carry out duties of state security that are placed within their competence by the law and regulations issued pursuant to the law ..." Please answer the following question: Are they professional organs only within the framework of those tasks of commands, units, institutions and staffs when it comes to carrying out jobs of state security?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They chiefly do or carry out tasks that you have cited within their units or the commands of their units. If during their work they collect information that pertain to some other units or to undermining the economic resources or political powers, then they forward that to their superior security organ for that organ to inform the competent authority that is more directly affected by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's take a look at pages 8 and 9 in English and page 8 in Serbian. We're interested in item 12. Thank you. So now you can see item 12. It says: "The security organs report on their work to their immediate superiors and the security organs of superior commands, units, institutions or staffs in accordance with the provision of these rules." Here is my question: Tell us, based on this, who these superior organs or the superior military officers of superior commands, or units, institutions or staffs are?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my case, my superior officer was the corps commander, or to name him, General Simic. And the superior organ was the chief of security sector of the General Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Take another look at line two. It says: "The security organs of superior commands." Are these the superior organs or the organs of the superior command? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are the security organs of that command. My superior commanding officer is the corps commander. When it comes to professional guidance and control, which was disputed before the break, my superior organ is the chief of the sector of security and intelligence of the General Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, let us take a look at page 10 in English and page 9 in Serbian. Item 16, which reads -- once you can see it, I'll read it out. Here it is. I quote item 16 from "Management of security organs. "The security organ is directly subordinated to the commanding officer of the command, unit, institution or staff of the armed forces in whose strength it is placed in the establishment, and it is responsible to that officer for its work ..." In your particular case, to whom were the security organs in the corps responsible for their work? To which officers, commanders?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have already answered in the previous question, I was responsible for my work and the state of security and intelligence support to the corps commander, or more specifically, to the commander of the East Bosnia Corps, General Simic. The security organs from my department were under my immediate jurisdiction. I had the right of guidance with regard to them or tasking them with individual tasks. The security organs in the brigades of the East Bosnia Corps were subordinate to the commander and reported exclusively to him, to the brigade commander, and my -- their relationship toward me was the same as my relationship toward the security organ and the superior command. Just as I was duty-bound to report and apply for approval from the chief of the security and intelligence sector of the Main Staff, in the same way the security organs in the brigades of the East Bosnia Corps were duty-bound to report to me and ask me for approval or forward some things for approval because my level wasn't authorised to give approval for the application of some special methods applied by the security organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's take a look at page 16 in Serbian and page 23 in English. Thank you. We're interested in article 57 so we can see what the level of the security administration does. Thank you. Thank you. We can see 57. We also have it in English. It says: "The Security Administration of the SSNO (hereinafter 'Security Administration') performs duties as prescribed by these rules and other regulations." Here's my question. Does it perform duties as prescribed by rules and other regulations, or others as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, did you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I was looking at the transcript. I didn't see the thank you part, because that's my -- that's my prompt to start my answer. Well, as you have read out, all security organs carried out their duties exclusively based on these rules of service and auxiliary regulations following from these rules and were issued and approved by the competent state authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic. Let's look at the second paragraph of 57. "The Security Administration provides specialist management for security organs in JNA commands ..." My question is this: Does this specialist management refer only to matters from the scope of work of the state security?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. State security and, if needed, it also includes matters pertaining to the military police and their engagement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Todorovic, let us look at item -- well, other items. Let's look at item 58: "The Security Administration provides specialist direction and co-ordination for the work of the security organs of the Territorial Defence ... " 59: "Individual counter-intelligence cases of particular interest and importance to the armed forces," which is part of their scope. Next, 60. Please turn the page. "The Security Administration is managed by the chief who is responsible to the Federal Secretary for National Defence ... " 61: "The security administration is responsible for the operative processing of all ... intelligence centres." In paragraph 2 of 61, it reads: "The Security Administration co-ordinates matters under paragraph 1 of this item with matters of the State Security Service of the federal administration organ competent for the interior ..." Can you explain what this refers to, these matters under paragraph 1, and what does it have to do with the State Security Service?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This has to do with detecting and documenting intelligence activity conducted by foreign armed forces and their services aimed at units and institutions of the JNA. Such centres and individuals were usually embedded in diplomatic, consular, and economic missions which legally existed in the territory of the former SFRY. If these were activities targeting members of the JNA, then it fell under the competence of the security administration of the JNA. However, most frequently there was a combination where interest was shown for economic, political, and other areas of interest. That is why co-ordination was necessary, which had to be well harmonised in order to carry out work jointly with members of the State Security Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic. You will recall having mentioned Mr. Radovic in your interview, who was with the State Security Service and their centre in Bijeljina. Can you tell the Chamber whether in keeping with the rules and regulations you -- were you duty-bound to co-operate with state security bodies in the field?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I had a fair professional co-operation with Mr. Radovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the rules foresee that you could exchange information with organs of akin services of the State Security Service and that this should be a two-way road in terms of exchange?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was envisaged in -- by the rules before us, specifically in one of its items. It specifies what security organ levels and what information can be exchanged with akin services. Such a service was also the State Security Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic. Let us look at item 67 of the rules before us. It enumerates all the competencies of the security administration. We'll read out only the first sentence of each item. "The security administration is responsible for specialist training ... Under (a), education; (b) programming and provision of materials. (C) monitors specialist training and research. 68, research and publishing. 69, equipping. 72: "The security administration prepares regulations on the work of security organs and the military police ..." and so on and so forth. Tell the Chamber whether while you were in the security administration you had to abide strictly by the laws and regulations when engaging in contact with anyone in the JNA who was not a member of security organs or with citizens or anyone else in the society.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had to. Of course, it refers to my professional specialist work and does not include private affairs. Even in the domain of private relationships, it was somewhat limited when contact with foreigners was concerned, but that was prescribed by a different rule. Such connections or relationships had to be documented. Anyone, in other words, engaged in the work of security organs had to abide by the regulations stemming from this -- from these rules, as well as by other general military regulation regulating the work, life, and conduct of all members of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we should come to an end for today. Can you please tell us your estimation for the length of your cross-examination tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We have announced the time we would require to examine the witness. We will abide by that limit, but if necessary, we may shorten the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is not the question I had put to you. We have to adjourn for today, and we'll resume tomorrow morning at 9.00 in this Courtroom number II. We adjourn.
